blocks.text: **The problem.** An array `nums` holds only the values `0`, `1` and `2` — think of them as red, white and blue. Sort it **in place** so all 0s come first, then all 1s, then all 2s. You may not use a library sort, and the follow-up asks for a **single pass**.

blocks.alt: Before: [2, 0, 2, 1, 1, 0] as blue, red, blue, white, white, red. After: [0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2] as two reds, two whites, two blues.

blocks.text: Example
Understanding the problem
This is a sort with a twist: there are only **three** possible values. A general sort takes O(n log n), but knowing the values in advance lets us do much better.
The puzzle is famous as the **Dutch national flag problem** (the Dutch flag is three horizontal stripes), posed by Edsger Dijkstra.
Approach 1: count, then overwrite
Count how many 0s, 1s and 2s there are, then write that many of each back into the array.
That's **O(n)** time and O(1) space — already good — but it walks the array **twice**. The follow-up asks: can we sort it while reading each element only once?
The key insight: four zones and three pointers
Keep the array split into four zones as you go. The 0s live at the front, the 2s at the back, the 1s in the middle — and one zone is still **unknown**. Three pointers mark the borders:

blocks.alt: The array split into four zones: 0s before low, 1s from low to mid, unknown from mid to high, and 2s after high.

blocks.text: `mid` looks at the first unknown value, and there are only three things it can be:

blocks.alt: Rules: if nums[mid] is 0, swap it with low and move low and mid forward. If it is 1, just move mid forward. If it is 2, swap it with high and move high back, but leave mid where it is.

elements.text: (mid stays: the value swapped in is unchecked)
elements.originalText: (mid stays: the value swapped in is unchecked)

blocks.text: The subtle rule is the last one. When we swap a 2 to the back, the value that comes from `high` hasn't been looked at yet — so `mid` must **not** move. When we swap a 0 to the front, the value coming from `low` is a 1 we've already checked (or it's the same element), so `mid` can safely move on.
We stop when `mid` passes `high`: the unknown zone is empty.
Dry run it yourself
Watch the three pointers squeeze the unknown zone from both ends. The tinted cells at each end are finished.

Complexity

blocks.alt: Counting: O(n) time over two passes, O(1) space. Dutch national flag: O(n) time in one pass, O(1) space.

blocks.text: Every step either moves `mid` forward or `high` backward, so the loop runs at most n times: **O(n) time, O(1) space**, in a single pass.

Where this idea shows up again

This three-way partition is exactly what makes quicksort fast on arrays with many repeated values ("3-way quicksort"). The same zone-and-pointer thinking also splits an array into negatives and positives, or evens and odds, in one pass.
